en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Food, 39.
The Training Rule on Luxurious Food.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, having requested exquisite foods for their own sake, ate them.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying:
"How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, request exquisite foods for their own sake and then eat them?"
"To whom is what is well-prepared not pleasing? To whom does what is delicious not appeal?
The monks heard those people complaining, grumbling, and expressing their indignation.
Those monks who were of few desires... [they] complained, grumbled, and expressed their indignation:
“How indeed can the group-of-six monks, having requested exquisite foods for their own sake, eat them?
… [and so on] … “Is it true, monks, that you, having requested exquisite foods for your own sake, eat them?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“…How, you foolish men, can you eat fine foods after having requested them for your own sake?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"Whatever fine foods there may be, such as ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses,
fish, meat, milk, and curd— whichever monk, for his own sake, [accepts] such fine foods..."
“If one eats after having requested [food], it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, the monks were ill.
The monks who were inquiring after the sick said this to the sick monks:
“We hope, friends, that you are bearing up; we hope that you are getting by?
“Formerly, friends, we used to request and eat fine foods for our own sake, and because of that we were comfortable.”
“But now, fearing we might be transgressing because it has been forbidden by the Blessed One, we do not request [it]; therefore, we have no ease.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow, monks, a sick monk to request for his own sake and eat choice foods.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
‘Now, those which are choice foods, namely: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses…’”
“Fish, meat, milk, and curd. Whatever monk, being not ill, should have such choice foods requested for his own sake and then eat them, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Now, as for those which are choice foods: [they are as follows:]...
Ghee means cow’s ghee, or goat’s ghee, or buffalo’s ghee; it is the ghee of those whose meat is permitted.
Fresh butter means...
Butter is just that [milk product].
Oil means sesame oil,
mustard seed oil, madhuka oil, castor oil, and fat oil.
"Madhu" means honey from bees.
"Phāṇitaṃ" means...
It is produced from sugarcane.
"Fish" is a term for water.
Meat means the meat of those animals whose meat is permitted.
Milk means...
Cow’s milk, or goat’s milk, or buffalo’s milk; the milk of those whose meat is permitted.
Curd means the curd of those same animals.
"But whoever" means whoever of such a kind... [as previously described] ...
"a bhikkhu."
...pe... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Such choice foods" refers to such kinds of choice foods.
"One who is not ill" means one for whom there is comfort even without choice foods.
"One who is ill" means...
For one who is not at ease without exquisite foods:
if, being not ill, he requests them for his own sake, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of requesting.
Upon receiving them, if he accepts them with the intention, "I shall eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing.
For every mouthful, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one who is not ill, perceiving himself as not ill, having requested exquisite foods for his own sake, eats them, there is an offense of expiation.
If one who is not ill, being doubtful, having requested exquisite foods for his own sake, eats them, there is an offense of expiation.
If one who is not ill, perceiving oneself as ill, requests fine foods for one's own sake and eats them, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one who is ill, perceiving oneself as not ill, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one who is ill, being in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if one is ill and perceives oneself as ill.
There is no offense for one who is ill.
Having requested [food] while being ill, one eats it when no longer ill;
or one eats the leftovers of one who is ill;
or from relatives.
When they have been invited,
for the sake of another,
with one's own wealth.
[This applies to] one who is insane,
or to the first offender.
The ninth training rule on exquisite food is finished.
